stories.original: **Australia brings non-bank lenders into open banking from November** *Australia's Consumer Data Right now covers non-bank lenders, extending mandatory data sharing to a sector that holds a significant share of the country's mortgage and consumer credit markets.* From July 13, eligible non-bank lenders in Australia must begin sharing product information under the Consumer Data Right (CDR) framework. Full consumer data sharing obligations follow from November. The expansion brings into scope a sector that has grown substantially since the CDR launched with the four major banks in 2020 and was extended to energy providers in 2022. The move is significant beyond Australia. European and UK policymakers wrestling with the scope of open finance frameworks face a similar question: whether to extend data-sharing obligations beyond deposit-taking institutions to non-bank credit providers. Australia's phased approach, beginning with product data before requiring consumer-level data sharing, offers one model for managing the compliance burden on smaller lenders. For European observers, the Australian experience will be instructive on two fronts: whether non-bank participation meaningfully improves switching and price competition in lending markets, and how smaller institutions manage the technical burden of compliance. *Sources: [Non-bank lenders brought into open banking regime from November | Australian Broker](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://www.brokernews.com.au/news/breaking-news/nonbank-lenders-brought-into-open-banking-regime-from-november-289643.aspx&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjVmNjkxZDEzNTU2NWU1MTc6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw1-KmXO63ULmfRQT2Tu890d) — Google Alert — open banking | [Non-banks begin product data sharing in CDR regime - Broker Daily](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://www.brokerdaily.au/regulation/21770-non-banks-begin-product-data-sharing-in-cdr-regime&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjVmNjkxZDEzNTU2NWU1MTc6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw2PGoDN-Gx3ZXukLumUvuME) — Google Alert — open banking | [Open banking expands as non-bank lenders join Consumer Data Right - Cyber Daily](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://www.cyberdaily.au/tech/13890-open-banking-expands-as-non-bank-lenders-join-consumer-data-right&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjVmNjkxZDEzNTU2NWU1MTc6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw1wKZ4fEFVlMeOZbfWtnuVi) — Google Alert — open banking | [Non-Bank Lenders Enter Consumer Data Right Stage | Mirage News](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://www.miragenews.com/non-bank-lenders-enter-consumer-data-right-stage-1708702/&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjVmNjkxZDEzNTU2NWU1MTc6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw1YtMcsSmR0pPI9DxllPZm8) — Google Alert — open banking*

**Mastercard considers selling its stake in UK payments firm Vocalink**

*A potential Vocalink sale would come as UK banks launch a domestic account-to-account scheme designed to reduce dependence on the card networks that currently underpin much of the country's payment infrastructure.*

Mastercard is examining a sale of Vocalink, the UK infrastructure operator that processes Faster Payments, Bacs and LINK ATM transactions, according to a report from Global Banking and Finance. Mastercard acquired Vocalink in 2017 for approximately £700 million, a deal that gave it control of the pipes through which the bulk of UK interbank payments flow.

The timing is notable. The UK Payments Initiative (UKPI) launched in June as a bank-backed domestic scheme explicitly designed to offer an alternative to Visa and Mastercard for retail payments. GoCardless became its first provider, and Moneyhub its first non-shareholder participant. If Mastercard is reassessing its ownership of Vocalink, it may reflect a judgement that the UK infrastructure's strategic value has shifted as the market moves towards new account-to-account rails.

A change of ownership would raise questions about governance and access terms for the UK's core payment infrastructure. Pay.UK, the operator that sits atop Vocalink's technology, is itself the subject of a government consultation on next-generation retail payments infrastructure. Any transaction would likely attract close scrutiny from the Payment Systems Regulator.

*Sources: [Mastercard Considers Sale of UK Payments Firm Vocalink Stake](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://www.globalbankingandfinance.com/mastercard-examines-sale-uk-payments-subsidiary-vocalink-ft/&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGmQ2MjhlZWE1MGQ0Zjk5YTU6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw2F31cPMfJicKlAyZmRc3bl) — Google Alert — payment systems regulator*

**Economist frames instant payments as front in US financial supremacy debate**

*A new analysis argues that domestic instant payment systems such as Brazil's Pix are emerging as geopolitical flashpoints, with US trade officials framing them as barriers to American financial services.*

The Economist has published an analysis examining threats to US financial supremacy, with domestic instant payment systems featuring prominently. The piece notes that US trade representative Jamieson Greer has complained that Pix, Brazil's instant payments system, unfairly disadvantages American payment companies, a framing that positions domestic payment infrastructure as a trade issue.

The argument has direct implications for Europe. The ECB's digital euro project, the EPI/Wero rollout, and the broader push for European payment autonomy, articulated recently by the Bank of Finland and the French Banking Federation, all rest on a similar logic: that domestic payment rails reduce dependence on foreign-owned networks. If the US begins treating such systems as trade barriers, European policymakers building sovereign payment infrastructure may face diplomatic pressure alongside the technical and commercial challenges they already confront.

The piece reflects a shift in how instant payments are discussed at policy level, from financial inclusion and efficiency tools to instruments of economic sovereignty and, potentially, trade friction.

*Sources: [Storm clouds gather over America's financial supremacy - The Economist](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2026/07/12/storm-clouds-gather-over-americas-financial-supremacy&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjQ2YzdlNzNlYWNlZDg4ZTE6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw2VGoed5YIp3F9pfrTGHsXD) — Google Alert — instant payments Europe*

**Lissi raises €3.5 million to build EUDI wallet infrastructure for financial services**

*The German digital identity firm is positioning its technology to support the European Digital Identity (EUDI) wallet framework, with applications spanning KYC, open finance and regulated data sharing.*

Lissi, a Berlin-based digital identity company, has raised €3.5 million to expand its infrastructure for the EU Digital Identity (EUDI) wallet. The company sees financial services as a primary use case, with its technology designed to support identity verification, KYC processes and the data-sharing models emerging under open finance regulation.

The EUDI wallet framework, mandated under the revised eIDAS regulation, is intended to give EU citizens a standardised way to prove their identity and share verified credentials across borders. For financial services, it offers a potential replacement for fragmented national KYC processes and a foundation for consent-based data sharing that complements PSD3 and the Financial Data Access (FiDA) regulation.

Lissi's fundraise is modest, but the company sits at an intersection that matters: identity infrastructure is a prerequisite for scalable open finance, and the firms building wallet-compatible verification tools now will shape how banks and fintechs onboard customers under the new framework.

*Sources: [Lissi Raises €3.5 Million To Expand EUDI Wallet Infrastructure For Europe's Financial Sector](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://pulse2.com/lissi-raises-e3-5-million-to-expand-eudi-wallet-infrastructure-for-europes-financial-sector/&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjgzMWYyODgyNDEyNDM0NTc6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw1sFRvmlpmOo7LnKzRbSTJJ) — Google Alert — open finance*

**Greek instant payments surged to 126 million transactions in 2025**

*IRIS, Greece's domestic instant payment system, processed €11 billion across 126 million transactions last year, underscoring the rapid adoption trajectory ahead of Greece's recent connection to the European instant payments network.*

Greece's IRIS instant payment system handled 126 million transactions worth €11 billion in 2025, according to data reported by Indicator.gr. The figures demonstrate strong domestic uptake, particularly among small businesses where instant payments are becoming embedded in everyday transactions.

The data provides useful context for Greece's connection to the European instant payments network via EuroPA, which went live earlier this month. That cross-border link means Greek consumers and businesses can now send and receive instant payments across the eurozone, extending the reach of a system that has already achieved meaningful domestic scale.

Greece's trajectory, from a late adopter of digital payments to a market processing over 100 million instant transactions annually, illustrates how quickly adoption can accelerate once infrastructure and regulatory conditions align. It also adds momentum to the European Commission's enforcement push on the instant payments regulation, with the first cases opened in June against member states lagging behind.

*Sources: [Surge in IRIS Payments in 2025: 126 Million Transactions Worth €11 Billion - Indicator.gr](https://www.google.com/url?rct=j&sa=t&url=https://indicator.gr/surge-in-iris-payments-in-2025-126-million-transactions-worth-e11-billion&ct=ga&cd=CAIyGjQ2YzdlNzNlYWNlZDg4ZTE6Y29tOmVuOlVT&usg=AOvVaw02psAnDy47oODi0TuAr0g5) — Google Alert — instant payments Europe*
